questions.stem: For Bayes' theorem to apply, the causes B1…Bk must be…
options: independent of each other and equal
mutually exclusive and also jointly exhaustive
equally likely and also mutually independent
dependent on each other and disjoint
questions.correctFeedback: Right — they must form a partition: no two can co-occur, and together they cover every possibility.
questions.incorrectFeedback: They must be mutually exclusive AND exhaustive — a partition. They need not be equally likely, and independence is a different idea entirely.

questions.stem: In Bayes' theorem, the denominator is exactly the same thing as…
options: the prior probability of the cause
the largest of the branch weights
the likelihood of the observed data
the total probability of the effect
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — the denominator is P(A), computed by the theorem of total probability as the sum of all branch weights.
questions.incorrectFeedback: It is P(A), the total probability of the effect: the sum of every branch weight. That is why the posterior is one branch's share of the total.

questions.stem: From Lesson 2: A and B are independent, with P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.4. Then P(A ∩ B) is…
questions.correctFeedback: Right — independence means P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2.
questions.incorrectFeedback: For independent events, multiply: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2. Adding gives P(A or B) only for events that can't overlap.

questions.stem: A positive result on an accurate test for a rare disease often still means…
options: the test itself must have been faulty somehow
the disease is far more common than said
a low posterior, because the prior was low
a high posterior, because the test is good
questions.correctFeedback: Exactly — the healthy majority produce so many false alarms that they swamp the true positives. The base rate dominates.
questions.incorrectFeedback: The posterior stays low. With a rare disease, the huge healthy group generates far more false positives than the small sick group generates true ones.
